QuestionStmt.S: If $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are integrable functions then $$\int f(x) \, dx \cdot \int g(x) \, dx =$$

Option3Stmt.S: $\int \left[ f(x) \int g(x) \, dx + g(x) \int f(x) \, dx \right] \, dx$

Option4Stmt.S: $\int \left[ f(x) \int g(x) \, dx - g(x) \int f(x) \, dx \right] \, dx$

Solution.S:
Step 1: Let $F(x) = \int f(x) \, dx$ and $G(x) = \int g(x) \, dx$. Then $F'(x) = f(x)$ and $G'(x) = g(x)$.

Step 2: We need to express $F(x) \cdot G(x)$. Using the product rule for differentiation:

$$\frac{d}{dx} [F(x) G(x)] = F'(x) G(x) + F(x) G'(x) = f(x) G(x) + F(x) g(x).$$

Step 3: Integrate both sides with respect to $x$:

$$F(x) G(x) = \int [f(x) G(x) + F(x) g(x)] \, dx.$$

Step 4: Substitute $F(x) = \int f(x) \, dx$ and $G(x) = \int g(x) \, dx$:

$$\int f(x) \, dx \cdot \int g(x) \, dx = \int \left[ f(x) \int g(x) \, dx + g(x) \int f(x) \, dx \right] \, dx.$$

Thus, the correct option is C.
